claim: To successfully guide limb movements, the brain takes in sensory information about the limb, internally tracks the state of the limb, and produces appropriate motor commands.
source: To successfully guide limb movements, the brain takes in sensory information about the limb, internally tracks the state of the limb, and produces appropriate motor commands.
evidence: This is a statement about established understanding of motor control processes, drawing from general scientific knowledge.

claim: The brain uses an internal model that describes prior beliefs about how the limb responds to motor commands.
source: It is widely believed that this process uses an internal model, which describes our prior beliefs about how the limb responds to motor commands.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: A mismatch between subjects' internal models and the actual BMI explains roughly 65% of movement errors.
source: We discovered that a mismatch between subjects' internal models and the actual BMI explains roughly 65% of movement errors, as well as long-standing deficiencies in BMI speed control.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 3C showing cross-validated angular errors.

claim: Internal model mismatch explains long-standing deficiencies in BMI speed control.
source: We discovered that a mismatch between subjects' internal models and the actual BMI explains roughly 65% of movement errors, as well as long-standing deficiencies in BMI speed control.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 comparing intended and actual cursor speeds.

claim: When we make a swift arm movement, the brain only knows where the arm was a split second ago, not where it currently is.
source: when we make a swift arm movement, the brain only knows where the arm was a split second ago, not where it currently is.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about sensory feedback delays in neural transmission.

claim: Internal models enable selection of appropriate motor commands and prediction of the outcomes of motor commands before sensory feedback becomes available.
source: To generate the desired movement, it is widely believed that we form internal models that enable selection of appropriate motor commands and prediction of the outcomes of motor commands before sensory feedback becomes available (Crapse and Sommer, 2008; Shadmehr et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: Mechanistic studies have made important progress toward identifying the neural circuits that implement internal models in sensory systems.
source: Mechanistic studies have made important progress toward identifying the neural circuits that implement internal models in sensory (Komatsu, 2006; Kennedy et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2014), vestibular (Laurens et al., 2013), and motor (Sommer, 2002; Ghasia et al., 2008; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009; Azim et al., 2014) systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Psychophysical studies have demonstrated the behavioral correlates of internal models.
source: In parallel, psychophysical studies have demonstrated the behavioral correlates of these internal models (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Wolpert et al., 1995; Thoroughman and Shadmehr, 2000; Kluzik et al., 2008; Mischiati et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Behavioral deficits result from lesions to brain areas involved in internal models.
source: and the behavioral deficits that result from lesions to corresponding brain areas (Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008; Bhanpuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous studies have provided strong evidence for the brain's use of internal models.
source: Together with studies showing neural correlates of internal models (Sommer, 2002; Gribble and Scott, 2002; Ghasia et al., 2008; Mulliken et al., 2008; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009; Green and Angelaki, 2010; Berkes et al., 2011; Laurens et al., 2013), these previous studies have provided strong evidence for the brain's use of internal models.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Most studies have viewed internal models through the lens of individual neurons or low-dimensional behavioral measurements.
source: However, to date, most studies have viewed internal models through the lens of individual neurons or low-dimensional behavioral measurements, which provides a limited view of these multi-dimensional neural processes (although see Berkes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on review of prior literature with citation to an exception.

claim: The study extracts a rich internal model from the activity of tens of neurons recorded simultaneously.
source: Here, we address these limitations by extracting a rich internal model from the activity of tens of neurons recorded simultaneously.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the current study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: An internal model is one's inner conception of a motor effector, which includes one's prior beliefs about the physics of the effector as well as how neural commands drive movements of the effector.
source: We define an internal model to be one's inner conception of a motor effector, which includes one's prior beliefs about the physics of the effector as well as how neural commands drive movements of the effector.
evidence: This is a definitional statement provided by the authors for the purposes of this study.

claim: A BMI represents a simplified and well-defined feedback control system, which facilitates the study of internal models.
source: A BMI represents a simplified and well-defined feedback control system, which facilitates the study of internal models (Golub et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents a rationale for the experimental approach.

claim: The BMI mapping from neural activity to movements is completely specified by the experimenter and can be chosen to define linear cursor dynamics.
source: In particular, the BMI mapping from neural activity to movements is completely specified by the experimenter and can be chosen to define linear cursor dynamics
evidence: This describes a property of the experimental design implemented in the study.

claim: In the BMI paradigm, relevant sensory feedback can be limited to one modality (vision).
source: the relevant sensory feedback can be limited to one modality (in this case, vision)
evidence: This describes a property of the experimental design.

claim: All neural activity that directly drives the BMI cursor is recorded.
source: and all neural activity that directly drives the cursor is recorded.
evidence: This describes a property of the experimental design.

claim: Subjects demonstrated proficient and stable control of the BMI, with success rates of nearly 100%.
source: Subjects indeed demonstrated proficient and stable control of the BMI, with success rates of nearly 100%, and movement times on average faster than one second (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Subjects demonstrated movement times on average faster than one second.
source: Subjects indeed demonstrated proficient and stable control of the BMI, with success rates of nearly 100%, and movement times on average faster than one second (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The visuomotor latency for monkey A was 100 ms.
source: The delays we measured (100 ms, monkey A; 133 ms, monkey C) are consistent with visuomotor latencies reported in arm reaching studies of single-neurons in primary motor cortex (Schwartz et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The visuomotor latency for monkey C was 133 ms.
source: The delays we measured (100 ms, monkey A; 133 ms, monkey C) are consistent with visuomotor latencies reported in arm reaching studies of single-neurons in primary motor cortex (Schwartz et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The measured visuomotor latencies are consistent with visuomotor latencies reported in arm reaching studies of single-neurons in primary motor cortex.
source: The delays we measured (100 ms, monkey A; 133 ms, monkey C) are consistent with visuomotor latencies reported in arm reaching studies of single-neurons in primary motor cortex (Schwartz et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to prior research cited.

claim: Motor commands pointed closer to the target when originating from the current cursor position than from outdated cursor positions.
source: we found that these error curves had minima at lags close to 0 ms (dashed black lines in Figure 2C), indicating that motor commands through the BMI mapping pointed closer to the targets when originating from the current cursor position than from any previous position.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Subjects use an internal model to internally predict the current cursor position.
source: This finding suggests that subjects use an internal model to internally predict the current cursor position.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on feedback delay compensation.

claim: Subjects' neural activity was often correct according to the internal model even when cursor movements were circuitous.
source: We found (i) that subjects' neural activity was often correct according to the internal model even when cursor movements were circuitous (thereby explaining 65% of cursor errors)
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Subjects intended to hold the cursor steadier during initial hold periods relative to observed behavior.
source: and (ii) that subjects intended to hold the cursor steadier during initial hold periods and to drive the cursor faster during movements, relative to observed behavior.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Subjects intended to drive the cursor faster during movements relative to observed behavior.
source: and (ii) that subjects intended to hold the cursor steadier during initial hold periods and to drive the cursor faster during movements, relative to observed behavior.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When the BMI mapping was perturbed, the subject's internal model changed in a manner consistent with the new BMI mapping.
source: Furthermore, when the BMI mapping was perturbed, the subject's internal model changed in a manner consistent with the new BMI mapping.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Internal models might not reside in M1.
source: Although internal models might not reside in M1 (Shadmehr, 1997; Pasalar et al., 2006; Miall et al., 2007; Mulliken et al., 2008; Lisberger, 2009), their computations influence activity in M1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Internal model computations influence activity in M1.
source: Although internal models might not reside in M1 (Shadmehr, 1997; Pasalar et al., 2006; Miall et al., 2007; Mulliken et al., 2008; Lisberger, 2009), their computations influence activity in M1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Two male rhesus macaques were each implanted with a 96-channel microelectrode array targeting proximal arm area of primary motor cortex.
source: Two male rhesus macaques (Maccaca mulatta) were each implanted with a 96-channel microelectrode array (Blackrock Microsystems, Salt Lake City, UT) targeting proximal arm area of primary motor cortex.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: In each session, 26.0 ± 3.4 neuronal units were recorded for monkey A.
source: In each session, we recorded 26.0 ± 3.4 (monkey A) and 39.2 ± 3.9 (monkey C) neuronal units (mean ± one standard deviation).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: In each session, 39.2 ± 3.9 neuronal units were recorded for monkey C.
source: In each session, we recorded 26.0 ± 3.4 (monkey A) and 39.2 ± 3.9 (monkey C) neuronal units (mean ± one standard deviation).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Spike counts were taken in nonoverlapping 33-ms bins throughout the behavioral task.
source: Spike counts were taken in nonoverlapping 33-ms bins throughout the behavioral task (see 'Behavioral task').
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology.

claim: All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Pittsburgh.
source: All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Pittsburgh.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: Extracted internal models explained roughly 65% of cursor movement errors (70%, monkey A; 59%, monkey C).
source: extracted internal models explained roughly 65% of cursor movement errors (70%, monkey A; 59%, monkey C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The majority of the explanatory power of extracted internal models was in their ability to identify structure in the high-dimensional neural activity.
source: We found that the majority of the explanatory power of extracted internal models was in their ability to identify structure in the high-dimensional neural activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Internal models fit to low-dimensional behavior rather than high-dimensional neural activity were not able to explain cursor errors.
source: Consistent with this finding, internal models fit to low-dimensional behavior rather than high-dimensional neural activity were not able to explain cursor errors (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This finding is supported by control analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Low intended speeds were systematically overestimated by the BMI mapping.
source: We found that low intended speeds were systematically overestimated, and high intended speeds were systematically underestimated by the BMI mapping (Figure 5A).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: High intended speeds were systematically underestimated by the BMI mapping.
source: We found that low intended speeds were systematically overestimated, and high intended speeds were systematically underestimated by the BMI mapping (Figure 5A).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Subjects intended to hold the cursor steadier during the initial hold period than what occurred during experiments.
source: Furthermore, we discovered that the subjects intended to hold the cursor steadier during the initial hold period and move the cursor faster during the movement than what occurred during experiments (Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Subjects intended to move the cursor faster during the movement than what occurred during experiments.
source: Furthermore, we discovered that the subjects intended to hold the cursor steadier during the initial hold period and move the cursor faster during the movement than what occurred during experiments (Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No assumptions were made about movement speed when extracting the internal model.
source: Note that we make no assumptions about movement speed when extracting the internal model (see the 'Framework for internal model estimation (IME)' subsection in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes a property of the methodological approach.

claim: Internal model mismatch limits realizable dynamic range of BMI movement speeds.
source: These systematic differences between intended and actual cursor speeds indicate that internal model mismatch limits realizable dynamic range of BMI movement speeds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on speed differences.

claim: Longstanding deficiencies in BMI speed control may be a consequence of internal model mismatch.
source: These findings suggest that the longstanding deficiencies in BMI speed control may be a consequence of internal model mismatch.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Arm reaching studies have demonstrated behavioral evidence of internal model adaptation.
source: Arm reaching studies have demonstrated behavioral evidence of internal model adaptation (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Thoroughman and Shadmehr, 2000; Joiner and Smith, 2008; Taylor et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Behavioral learning has been demonstrated in the context of BMIs.
source: Behavioral learning has also been demonstrated in the context of BMIs (Taylor, 2002; Carmena et al., 2003; Jarosiewicz et al., 2008; Ganguly and Carmena, 2009; Chase et al., 2012; Sadtler et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Extracted internal models adapted in a manner consistent with the BMI perturbations.
source: Our key finding in this analysis is that extracted internal models adapted in a manner consistent with the BMI perturbations (Figure 6B).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: During the perturbation trials, the time-varying internal model adapted to better match the perturbed BMI mapping.
source: During the perturbation trials, the time-varying internal model adapted to better match the perturbed BMI mapping (red trace trends toward zero).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: During the washout trials, the time-varying internal model adapted to better match the intuitive BMI mapping.
source: Similarly, during the washout trials, the time-varying internal model adapted to better match the intuitive BMI mapping (blue trace trends toward zero).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Internal model mismatch was present throughout the intuitive, perturbation, and washout trials.
source: Consistent with our central hypothesis, internal model mismatch was present throughout the intuitive, perturbation, and washout trials.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The subject's internal model was stable throughout the intuitive session.
source: The subject's internal model was stable throughout the intuitive session, as evidenced by the nearly constant angular differences between velocities mapped through the time-varying internal model and the BMI mapping (red and blue traces are roughly flat in Figure 6B)
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Behavioral performance was stable throughout the intuitive trials.
source: Consistent with a stable internal model, behavioral performance was stable throughout the intuitive trials (blue trace is flat in Figure 6A)
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The neural activity recorded in M1 is likely to be downstream of the internal model computations.
source: First, the neural activity recorded in M1 is likely to be downstream of the internal model computations, whether they be in cerebellum (Shadmehr, 1997; Pasalar et al., 2006; Miall et al., 2007; Lisberger, 2009; Huang et al., 2013), posterior parietal cortex (Shadmehr, 1997; Mulliken et al., 2008), dorsal premotor cortex (Shadmehr, 1997), or elsewhere.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature about neural circuits.

claim: Internal copy signals carry information about movement intent, in particular a copy of the movement intent that M1 sends to the motor effector.
source: Second, previous studies indicate that internal copy signals (e.g., efference copy, corollary discharge) carry information about movement intent, in particular a copy of the movement intent that M1 sends to the motor effector (Crapse and Sommer, 2008; Huang et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2014; Azim et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The authors chose to capture the subject's internal model using a forward model framework because it is both highly interpretable and consistent with a large body of behavioral and computational studies.
source: We chose to capture the subject's internal model using a forward model framework (Equation 2 and Figure 3A) because it is both highly interpretable and consistent with a large body of behavioral and computational studies (Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008; Frens, 2009).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the methodological choice, supported by citations.

claim: Extracted internal models explain a majority of behavioral errors on trials not seen during model fitting.
source: First, extracted internal models explain a majority of behavioral errors on trials not seen during model fitting (Figure 3C).
evidence: This finding is supported by cross-validated experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The finding that intended speed is better predicted by internal models than the BMI mapping lends an additional independent validation of those internal models.
source: Second, the finding that intended speed is better predicted by internal models than the BMI mapping (Figure 5B) lends an additional independent validation of those internal models, since no assumptions were made about intended movement speed when fitting internal models.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When the BMI mapping was perturbed, extracted internal models revealed adaptation consistent with the particular perturbations.
source: Third, when we perturbed the BMI mapping, extracted internal models revealed adaptation consistent with the particular perturbations (Figure 6).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The data are not consistent with two versions of the alternative hypothesis, in which the subject's internal model is well-matched to the BMI mapping.
source: We showed that our data are not consistent with two versions of the alternative hypothesis, in which the subject's internal model is well-matched to the BMI mapping (Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This finding is supported by control analysis data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: Subjects could readily produce the full range of movement directions through the BMI mapping.
source: Although M1 cannot readily produce all possible patterns of high-dimensional neural activity (Sadtler et al., 2014), we observed that subjects could readily produce the full range of movement directions through the BMI mapping (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Gaps between producible movement directions were typically less than 1/4 of a degree.
source: Gaps between producible movement directions were typically less than 1/4 of a degree, which is substantially smaller than the cursor errors shown in Figure 3C.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The main finding of internal model mismatch cannot be explained by subjects' inability to produce particular neural activity patterns.
source: This suggests that our main finding of internal model mismatch cannot be explained by subjects' inability to produce particular neural activity patterns.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on producible movement directions.

claim: Simulated neural activity was more consistent with the BMI mapping than the extracted internal model.
source: However, this was not the case. Simulated neural activity was more consistent with the BMI mapping than the extracted internal model, which contrasts with our finding from the recorded neural activity.
evidence: This finding is from simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: All findings presented throughout this paper are cross-validated.
source: To rule out this possibility, all findings presented throughout this paper are cross-validated (see the 'Computing cross-validated internal model predictions' subsection in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used throughout the study.

claim: Internal models explained the majority of cursor errors in the held-out data.
source: However, this was not the case. Internal models explained the majority of cursor errors in the held-out data (Figure 3C), demonstrating that extracted internal models captured real, task-relevant structure in the recorded neural activity.
evidence: This finding is supported by cross-validated experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Internal models extracted from shuffled data sets could no longer explain cursor errors.
source: However, internal models extracted from these shuffled data sets could no longer explain cursor errors, indicating that IME does not identify effects when they do not exist in the data.
evidence: This finding is supported by control analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: The majority of the explanatory power of extracted internal models relies on structure in the high-dimensional neural activity.
source: This result is consistent with our findings that the majority of the explanatory power of extracted internal models relies on structure in the high-dimensional neural activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cursor errors cannot be explained by internal models when high-dimensional neural activity is replaced by low-dimensional behavioral measurements during model fitting.
source: and that cursor errors cannot be explained by internal models when high-dimensional neural activity is replaced by low-dimensional behavioral measurements during model fitting (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This finding is supported by control analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: A major limitation in BMI performance is the ability to control cursor speed.
source: A major limitation in BMI performance is the ability to control cursor speed (Gilja et al., 2012; Golub et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gilja et al. (2012) and Golub et al. (2014) have proposed solutions to improve control of BMI speed.
source: Gilja et al. (2012) and Golub et al. (2014) have proposed solutions to improve control of BMI speed (in particular, with respect to stopping the BMI cursor at targets).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The subject's learning process may be a key limitation in BMI performance.
source: Nevertheless, our findings indicate that the subject's learning process may be a key limitation in BMI performance (Sadtler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings, with citation to related work.

claim: It may be possible to overcome limitations in the subject's neural adaptation process through complementary innovations in designing the BMI mapping.
source: It may be possible to overcome these limitations in the subject's neural adaptation process through complementary innovations in designing the BMI mapping (Shenoy and Carmena, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications, with citation.

claim: Applying an extracted internal model as the BMI mapping might improve performance during closed-loop BMI control.
source: For example, applying an extracted internal model as the BMI mapping might improve performance during closed-loop BMI control.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: A recent study incorporating the concept of internal tracking has demonstrated substantial gains in closed-loop BMI performance.
source: Indeed, a recent study incorporating the concept of internal tracking has demonstrated substantial gains in closed-loop BMI performance (Gilja et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The insights gained in this study were made possible because the authors monitored the subject's high-dimensional neural activity.
source: The insights gained in this study were made possible because we monitored the subject's high-dimensional neural activity.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological approach that enabled the findings.

claim: Neural activity that was consistently correct under the internal model sometimes resulted in aberrant behavior through the BMI mapping.
source: Because the BMI mapping and the subject's internal model are high-to-low dimensional mappings, neural activity that was consistently correct under the internal model sometimes resulted in aberrant behavior through the BMI mapping.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The authors would not have been able to observe or explain the phenomenon of internal model mismatch by analyzing the BMI cursor movements in isolation.
source: We would not have been able to observe or explain this phenomenon by analyzing the BMI cursor movements in isolation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an inference supported by control analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Access to the high-dimensional neural activity enabled the identification of the subject's intended movements without constraining them to have a consistent relationship with actual movements.
source: In contrast, access to the high-dimensional neural activity enabled the identification of the subject's intended movements without constraining them to have a consistent relationship with actual movements.
evidence: This is an inference about the methodological advantage of the approach.

claim: Prior beliefs and their role in sensation and behavior have been the focus of many studies on visual perception.
source: Prior beliefs, and their role in sensation and behavior, have been the focus of many studies, including those on visual perception (Kersten et al., 2004; Komatsu, 2006; Berkes et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Prior beliefs and their role in sensation and behavior have been the focus of many studies on perceptual decision-making.
source: Prior beliefs, and their role in sensation and behavior, have been the focus of many studies, including those on visual perception (Kersten et al., 2004; Komatsu, 2006; Berkes et al., 2011), perceptual decision-making (Ma and Jazayeri, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Prior beliefs and their role in sensation and behavior have been the focus of many studies on sensorimotor learning.
source: Prior beliefs, and their role in sensation and behavior, have been the focus of many studies, including those on visual perception (Kersten et al., 2004; Komatsu, 2006; Berkes et al., 2011), perceptual decision-making (Ma and Jazayeri, 2014), and sensorimotor learning (Körding and Wolpert, 2004; Turnham et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Outwardly aberrant behavior and behavioral limitations could be explained by taking into account the subject's prior beliefs.
source: We found that outwardly aberrant behavior and behavioral limitations could be explained by taking into account the subject's prior beliefs.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the experimental findings.

claim: By recording simultaneously from multiple neurons and developing the appropriate statistical algorithms, it may be possible to extract similarly rich prior beliefs in other systems.
source: By recording simultaneously from multiple neurons and developing the appropriate statistical algorithms, it may be possible to extract similarly rich prior beliefs in other systems.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications of the methodology.
